subtitle: Midterm Important Subjective Questions (Solved)
topics: Web Tools and Games for Language Learning

subjective.question: What is CALL? Define it briefly.
subjective.answer: CALL stands for Computer-Assisted Language Learning. It refers to the use of computer technology — including software, multimedia, the Internet and mobile tools — to support, practise and enhance the teaching and learning of languages.

subjective.question: How does the use of technology make learning learner-centred?
subjective.answer: Technology makes learning learner-centred because learners can choose material suited to their level, learn at their own pace, practise independently and take an active part in the learning process instead of only listening to the teacher. The teacher's role changes from a lecturer to a facilitator who guides and supports the learners.

subjective.question: What are the benefits of using technology in language teaching?
subjective.answer: The main benefits are: (1) it increases learners' motivation and interest; (2) it provides alternative and varied ways of teaching and learning; (3) it expands opportunities for learning beyond the classroom; (4) it helps learners learn meaningfully through authentic material; (5) it develops learners' emotions, cooperation and communication; and (6) it makes the language class an active place.

subjective.question: How does technology increase learners' motivation?
subjective.answer: Technology increases motivation because multimedia material is interesting and attractive, learners can interact with the material and with other people, and they can see their progress immediately. The combination of multimedia and technology attracts students' attention, and the use of the Internet further increases learners' motivation to learn the language.

subjective.question: What is multimedia? Discuss its role in language teaching.
subjective.answer: Multimedia is the combination of text, sound, images, animation and video in learning material. It attracts students' attention, presents language in a meaningful context, and involves more senses in the learning process. Because more senses are involved, learning becomes more durable and learners can understand and remember the topic more easily.

subjective.question: How does the use of film help in language teaching?
subjective.answer: Film presents language in its real, natural context, so it helps learners realize the topic and understand how the language is actually used. It provides authentic language input, shows the culture of the target language, attracts learners' attention and makes the lesson interesting and meaningful.

subjective.question: Discuss the role of the Internet in language learning.
subjective.answer: The Internet gives learners access to authentic materials, up-to-date information and real communication with other speakers of the language. It increases learners' motivation, expands opportunities for learning, supports independent learning, and has become a part of the social phenomenon of modern life, so learners use the language for real purposes.

subjective.question: How can cooperation among learners be enhanced through technology?
subjective.answer: Cooperation is one of the most important tools for learning. With computer technology, learners can work together on tasks, share ideas, and communicate through chat, forums and collaborative tools. In this way learners' cooperation can be enhanced through technology, and they learn from each other while using the language meaningfully.

subjective.question: Describe Warschauer's three phases of CALL.
subjective.answer: Warschauer divides the history of CALL into three phases: (1) Behaviouristic CALL (1970s–1980s), in which the computer was used as a tutor for drill and practice; (2) Communicative CALL (1980s–1990s), which focused on using the language in communication rather than only practising forms; and (3) Integrative CALL (21st century), which integrates the language skills through multimedia and the Internet.

subjective.question: Differentiate between synchronous and asynchronous communication in language learning.
subjective.answer: Synchronous communication takes place in real time, for example chat and video conferencing, in which all participants are present at the same time. Asynchronous communication does not require the participants to be present at the same time, for example e-mail and discussion forums, in which learners can read and reply whenever they want. Both are forms of computer-mediated communication (CMC) used in language learning.

subjective.question: Why is a technology-enhanced teaching environment effective for learners?
subjective.answer: Technology-enhanced teaching environments are effective for learners because they offer alternative ways of learning, immediate feedback, individual practice at the learner's own pace and access to rich authentic input. The positive effect of technology, however, depends on its usage: it is the way the teacher and learners use the technology that makes it effective.

subjective.topic: Web Tools and Games for Language Learning
subjective.question: What is Web 2.0? How is it useful for language learners?
subjective.answer: Web 2.0 refers to the second generation of the World Wide Web, in which users are not only readers but also creators of content. A Web 2.0 site allows users to interact and collaborate as creators — for example through blogs, wikis and social networking sites. In language learning, this means learners can produce, publish and share language content and communicate with a real audience.

subjective.topic: Web Tools and Games for Language Learning
subjective.question: Name and explain different categories of tools used in language teaching, with one example each.
subjective.answer: Common categories are: office tools, such as PowerPoint, used for preparing and presenting material; chat tools, such as Telegram, used for real-time communication; news tools, such as Nuzzel, used for collecting and reading news; and gaming tools, such as Hot Potatoes, used for creating and playing learning games and exercises.

subjective.topic: Web Tools and Games for Language Learning
subjective.question: What is Hot Potatoes? How is it used in language teaching?
subjective.answer: Hot Potatoes is a gaming/authoring tool used by teachers to create interactive exercises such as quizzes, cloze activities, crosswords, matching and ordering exercises (through modules such as JQuiz, JCloze, JMatch and JCross). These exercise-games make practice interesting, give immediate feedback and help learners revise the language in an enjoyable way.

subjective.topic: Web Tools and Games for Language Learning
subjective.question: How can chat tools like Telegram be used in language learning?
subjective.answer: Chat tools such as Telegram allow learners to communicate in the target language in real time. They encourage learners to write and respond quickly, practise informal language, ask questions and work with partners or groups outside the classroom. In this way chat tools make technology an interactive tool in language learning.

subjective.topic: Web Tools and Games for Language Learning
subjective.question: Discuss the role of video games in ESL learning.
subjective.answer: Video games involve learners actively in the language, provide language practice in a meaningful context and are highly motivating. Educational ESL games, such as 'Heart of Tota', present vocabulary and structures through play. It is even suggested that video game addicts should play ESL games, so that their gaming habit also develops their English.

subjective.topic: Web Tools and Games for Language Learning
subjective.question: What is meant by the 'Everest Syndrome' in technology use?
subjective.answer: The 'Everest Syndrome' refers to a situation of the use of specific technology — technology is used in teaching simply because it is available and impressive, like climbing Mount Everest 'because it is there', rather than because it serves a clear learning purpose. Teachers should avoid this and select technology according to their learners' needs and teaching objectives.

subjective.question: What is a virtual world? Give its main features.
subjective.answer: A virtual world (VW) is an online, computer-simulated 3D environment in which users, represented by avatars, can interact with the environment and with each other. Virtual worlds are primarily social spaces created for the purpose of human interaction, and an online 3D environment may simulate the real world.

subjective.question: Write a short note on the creation of MUD.
subjective.answer: In 1978, Roy Trubshaw, a student at the University of Essex, created a new game patterned on one of the variations of Zork, which he called MUD (Multi-User Dungeon). He developed it further with Richard Bartle. MUD was a text-based virtual environment in which many users could log in at the same time, explore the world and interact with each other through written text.

subjective.question: What is a MOO? How is it different from a MUD?
subjective.answer: MOO stands for 'MUD, Object-Oriented'. It is a text-based virtual world developed from MUD in which the environment is built from programmable objects. Users communicate through written text, and they can create objects, rooms and activities themselves, which makes MOOs useful for language learning and teaching.

subjective.question: Discuss the origin of text-based virtual environments with reference to the Mammoth Cave system.
subjective.answer: The first virtual text-based environment was based on the real-life Mammoth Cave system in Kentucky, USA. It was the game Colossal Cave Adventure, created by Will Crowther, in which the player explored a cave system through text descriptions and commands. It became the model for later text-based virtual worlds such as Zork and MUD.

subjective.question: Write a note on Active Worlds and its educational significance.
subjective.answer: Active Worlds (AWs), created in 1995, was one of the first widely available virtual worlds with a significant education component. It allows users to explore and build 3D virtual environments through their avatars. In education, it has been used for virtual campuses, simulations and collaborative projects in which learners interact and learn in an immersive environment.

subjective.question: Why do Steinkuehler and Williams consider virtual worlds as 'new third spaces'?
subjective.answer: Steinkuehler and Williams consider virtual worlds as 'new third spaces'. Following the idea of the 'third place' — an informal social place outside home (first place) and work (second place) — they argue that virtual worlds are important social spaces where people meet, socialize and form communities. This social nature is what makes virtual worlds valuable for language practice.

subjective.question: What are the benefits of virtual worlds for language learners?
subjective.answer: Virtual worlds benefit language learners in several ways: (1) they provide opportunities for real-life communication practice with other speakers; (2) they expose learners to the real world via the virtual environment; (3) they are highly motivating and encourage learners to use the language for real purposes; and (4) they create a social space in which learners can practise without the fear of face-to-face mistakes.

subjective.question: How have virtual worlds developed since their early days?
subjective.answer: In the early days of VW development, the choices were quite limited: virtual worlds were mostly text-based, graphics and facilities were simple, and few people had access to them. With the development of 3D graphics and the Internet, virtual worlds became richer and more widely available, and research interest grew — studies examining VWs have almost entirely been published after 2000.

subjective.question: What difficulties do researchers face in studying virtual worlds?
subjective.answer: Researchers face several difficulties in studying virtual worlds. It is quite difficult to determine how many individuals are making use of VWs, because users may join from anywhere in the world, use different names and avatars, and enter or leave at any time. Their activities are also spread over large virtual spaces, which makes observation and data collection difficult.
